Industrial civilization is not merely “one way of living” among many; it is a planetary metabolism built on extraction, conversion, and waste at scales that overwhelm the Earth’s ability to regenerate. Its defining technologies—fossil-fuel energy systems, industrial agriculture, global supply chains, mass manufacturing, and the digital-industrial surveillance stack that coordinates them—do not sit atop nature as neutral tools. They reorganize land, water, climate, and living communities into inputs for a machine whose basic requirement is perpetual growth. If ecological balance and genuine human freedom are the goals, then reform is not enough. The core machinery must be dismantled, and humanity must deliberately step down from industrial-scale power toward small, place-based, pre-agricultural lifeways—ways of living that evolved within ecological limits rather than against them.

1) Industrial civilization is structurally incompatible with ecological stability

The environmental crisis is often framed as a list of “side effects”: carbon emissions, biodiversity loss, plastic pollution, deforestation, soil erosion. But those are not accidental. They follow inevitably from the industrial project itself: converting complex, living systems into simplified production zones.

  • Energy abundance drives total throughput. Industrialism’s superpower is concentrated energy (historically coal, oil, gas). That energy doesn’t just “run devices”; it multiplies mining, logging, shipping, and mechanized agriculture, turning entire regions into sacrifice zones. Even when a technology appears “clean” at the point of use, the industrial web behind it (mines, smelters, roads, ports, data centers) expands the human footprint.
  • Industrial agriculture is ecological liquidation. Monocultures, synthetic fertilizers, pesticides, and irrigation transform soil into a medium for commodity output rather than a living community. This breaks nutrient cycles, collapses insect and bird populations, depletes aquifers, and drives deforestation. The problem is not a few bad practices; it’s the agricultural-industrial imperative to maximize yield for markets rather than resilience for ecosystems.
  • Complex technology depends on global extraction. Modern technological systems require rare metals, petrochemicals, high-temperature processing, and planet-spanning logistics. Even “green” high-tech depends on intensive mining and industrial infrastructure. A civilization that must continuously excavate the Earth to maintain itself is, by definition, ecologically unstable.

Pre-agricultural lifeways—mobile or semi-mobile foraging, hunting, fishing, and gathering, embedded in local ecologies—have one overwhelming advantage: they are constrained by immediate feedback. When people live within the rhythms of a watershed, a forest, a coastline, the consequences of overuse are visible and personal. Industrial society insulates consumers from those consequences through distance, markets, and bureaucracy. Ecological balance requires the restoration of feedback—limits that can be felt, not merely calculated.

2) “Sustainability” within industrialism is a contradiction

Many propose a middle path: keep industrial civilization, but power it differently, regulate it better, and make it more efficient. This misunderstands how industrial systems behave.

  • Efficiency often increases total consumption. When processes become cheaper and faster, societies tend to expand them—more production, more travel, more devices, more extraction. This is not a moral failure of individuals; it is a structural outcome of growth economics.
  • Global systems externalize costs. Industrial society survives by pushing harm elsewhere: to distant lands, future generations, nonhuman life. As long as the system’s success is measured in output and growth, it will treat ecological integrity as a barrier to be managed.
  • High-tech “solutions” perpetuate the same mindset. Geoengineering, mass electrification without de-growth, and ever more complex control systems assume that the right machinery can override planetary boundaries. That is the same mentality that created the crisis: the belief that nature is a problem to be engineered rather than a community to belong to.

If the machine’s operating principle is permanent expansion, then calling for industrial civilization to become ecologically balanced is like asking a fire to become cold. The honest response is to extinguish the fire—carefully, deliberately, and with full awareness of what it has displaced.

3) Industrial life erodes authentic human existence

The argument for dismantling industrialism is not only ecological. It is also about what modern systems do to the human animal.

  • Alienation is not incidental; it is engineered. Industrial society separates people from food sources, from land, from practical competence, and from the direct social bonds required to survive. In exchange, it offers mediated substitutes: consumption, entertainment, and institutional dependence.
  • Technological systems concentrate power. Large-scale infrastructure—grids, networks, factories, bureaucracies—requires centralized control. This makes ordinary people legible, manageable, and replaceable. “Convenience” often functions as a soft form of coercion: if you cannot meet your needs without the system, you cannot freely refuse it.
  • Psychological health suffers under abstraction. Human beings evolved in small bands with immediate consequences, tangible work, deep familiarity with place, and constant social reciprocity. Industrial life replaces this with symbolic labor, screens, and anonymity. The resulting epidemics of loneliness, anxiety, and purposelessness are not mysterious; they are symptoms of a mismatch between our evolved nature and our manufactured environment.

Pre-agricultural lifeways, by contrast, are not “primitive” in the sense of being simplistic. They are sophisticated forms of ecological intelligence: reading tracks, seasons, plant cycles; negotiating social relationships; sharing risk; maintaining cultural knowledge through story and practice. They cultivate autonomy and belonging not as ideals, but as necessities.

4) The moral case: ending a way of life that requires mass harm

Industrial civilization’s comforts are purchased with harms that are systematically hidden: exploited labor, devastated landscapes, poisoned rivers, extinct species, and a destabilized climate that will punish the poor first and hardest. A society that must inflict large-scale, involuntary suffering in order to function is not “advanced.” It is ethically indefensible.

Moreover, industrial civilization does not merely damage ecosystems; it displaces other lifeways—especially Indigenous and subsistence cultures that have historically maintained long-term relationships with their lands. Dismantling industrial systems is therefore also a matter of justice: making space for many forms of human life, rather than enforcing one global monoculture of production and consumption.

5) A return to pre-agricultural lifeways is the clearest path to rebalancing the Earth

“Return” does not have to mean naïve reenactment or romanticizing hardship. It means re-centering human life on ecological participation rather than industrial domination.

A pre-agricultural orientation offers:

  • Low throughput by design. When your energy comes from muscle, fire, local materials, and human-scale tools, your impact is naturally bounded.
  • Biodiversity as a partner, not an obstacle. Foragers thrive in diverse ecosystems; they have an incentive to keep landscapes rich and resilient rather than simplified.
  • Resilience through redundancy and local knowledge. Industrial systems are fragile: they depend on uninterrupted flows of fuel, parts, and information. Small-scale lifeways distribute risk and rely on skills and relationships that do not collapse when a distant supply chain breaks.

Industrial society engenders alienation—from community, from meaningful work, from natural landscapes, and from ourselves. Rising rates of mental illness, loneliness, and stress epidemics testify to this disconnection. While technology offers entertainment and fleeting satisfaction, it atomizes human relationships and distracts from deeper fulfillment rooted in purpose and connection to the earth.

Moreover, the hierarchy and coercion necessary to maintain large, complex societies undermine freedom and egalitarianism. Pre-agricultural hunter-gatherer societies—far from being “nasty, brutish, and short,” as outdated myths contend—were often egalitarian, cooperative, and deeply embedded in their environments, fostering resilient, meaningful communities. Their lifeways exemplify a human existence characterized by autonomy, social harmony, and intimacy with nature—qualities eroded under civilization’s crushing weight.

Returning to Pre-Agricultural Lifeways: An Ethical and Pragmatic Choice

Critics argue that abandoning civilization would mean chaos or suffering. Yet evidence from anthropology undermines these fears. For hundreds of thousands of years, humans lived as nomadic foragers within vibrant ecosystems, sustaining themselves without degrading the land or requiring authoritarian structures. Their smaller, dispersed populations allowed for regeneration of plant and animal communities, creating a balance now obliterated by industrial expansion.

Rewilding humanity—recovering these lifeways—thus offers a path toward restoring ecological integrity. While the dismantling of civilization is undoubtedly disruptive, the alternative—continuing on our current trajectory—is far more catastrophic: ecological collapse, social fragmentation, and existential despair.

The complete dismantling of industrial civilization—returning to pre-agricultural, place-based, low-impact lifeways—is not only the most ethical response but perhaps our only hope of restoring ecological balance and rediscovering authentic human existence. It is time, at last, for humanity to come home.
